result.delta_one_sentence: A aligns a fixed subword tokenizer's tokens directly and uses the resulting one-to-one ratio and aligner score to predict downstream cross-lingual transfer, while B keeps the alignment at the word level, uses it only to define crossing-free cuts, and scores where byte-level models' learned chunk boundaries fall, normalized between a shift null and a ceiling with the same boundary budget and rate-calibrated to separate boundary rate from boundary placement, all to make a go/no-go decision about training rather than to predict transfer.
result.reasoning:
Shared idea: both use a statistical word aligner on professionally translated parallel text to ask whether a model's segmentation lines up across languages. The mechanisms differ in four ways.
(1) What is aligned. A runs the aligner on the tokenizer's own subword tokens and reads correspondence from the link structure (share of one-to-one links, max log-probability). B runs a frozen aligner on untokenized words, turns the links into phrase-consistent cut positions, and treats model boundaries as point events scored against those cuts.
(2) What is segmented. A studies static subword vocabularies such as BPE or unigram. B studies the dynamic, learned boundary predictors of byte-level models, plus the byte and character canonicalization they need.
(3) Statistic and controls. A's one-to-one ratio mixes boundary rate with placement, and A admits it drops when the source is over-segmented. A's second score is an unnormalized aligner likelihood that has no null. B builds the rate-versus-placement split in from the start: a Dice score normalized between a circular-shift floor and a ceiling with the same budget, native versus rate-calibrated boundaries, a check with two aligners from different families, and a monolingual segmentation reference.
(4) Output. A gives a correlational predictor checked against transfer and retrieval across many models, scripts and tokenizer types. B gives a pre-registered stop-or-headroom verdict and trains no model.

Why A is the stronger contribution: it ties its metric to outcomes people care about. Rank correlation with transfer, retrieval and embedding alignment across encoders, decoders and both same-script and cross-script pairs makes it a reusable finding with external validity. A has real weaknesses. It is correlational and likely confounded by language relatedness and resource size. A single aligner iteration with an unnormalized max log-probability is an odd, uncalibrated score. Its claim to support fairer tokenizers is asserted, not tested.
B is the more careful measurement design. Its nulls and ceilings, rate calibration and pre-registered decision rule are better than A's. But its scope is narrow: few released byte-level models, English-centred pairs, and no downstream link. Its deliverable is an internal feasibility gate whose "stop" branch is a modest negative result.
So A is the stronger contribution as a finding, while B has the better methodology for its narrower question.

largest_defect: Identification and instrument validity at the registered decision point. The registered primary verdict is read on EN-ZH, stage 1, with the Chinese side rate-calibrated to the English stage-1 count. By the proposal's own premises (C04 and M6: Chinese stage-1 chunks are about one character; the H-Net paper 2507.07955 Table 4 gives Chinese 2-stage BPIC 5.81 at a (3,3) target; S2 bytes per sentence EN 130, ZH 125), the Chinese side then covers about 0.85-1.0 of its canonical gaps. The floor circularly shifts only side b (compute/instrument_sim.py pbd_record: shift(bb, k), confirmed by the recorder), so it collapses onto the system, and (ceiling - floor) shrinks toward zero. S is then driven by Chinese density and the English side's word-end miss rate, not by translation-specific placement: with perfect Chinese placement, the identification refuter (seeds 42/43/44) and reviewer 1 (seed 42) both found S near 1 with no English miss but about 0.78-0.82 (a HEADROOM call) with a 3% miss at density about 0.89-0.92, while the same 3% miss at density 0.54 gives 0.947; near saturation S leaves [0, 1] (1.156) or is NaN. A 3% miss therefore moves S by about 0.18-0.2 against the 0.03 gap between the decision lines (0.88 and 0.85). Every threshold and the agreement gate were tuned on S1 operating characteristics in a different regime (a budget near the consistent-cut count plus 2% extras; independent aligner errors at link AER 0.03-0.13), and no registered gate (I1-I6) catches the collapse (I1 cannot fail because a permuted alignment leaves about 0.05 cuts per sentence; line M at its own budget saturates trivially). So NO_HEADROOM, HEADROOM and HEADROOM_MONOLINGUAL are not identified at the operating point. Both reviewers name this defect: reviewer 1 (claude-opus-5-5, 52, the authoritative score) as its single largest defect, with a repair; reviewer 2 (qwen3.6-35b-a3b, 57) as the first half of its largest defect, together with the broken code stack. Ranked second: aligner-noise realism (published unsupervised EN-ZH AER for the chosen aligner families is about 0.18-0.27, and CTFAlign and SimAlign share an extraction lineage, so under correlated errors the feasibility refuter's rerun of S1's own decision code never returns NO_HEADROOM and returns HEADROOM with probability 1 at true S 0.90-0.96). Third, and cheap to repair: the registered compute does not run on the pinned stack (fp32 with TF32 off against hnet mha.py's fp16/bf16 flash-attention asserts; mamba_ssm@a6a1dae imports GreedySearchDecoderOnlyOutput, which transformers 5.15.0 no longer exports; both verified by reviewer 1 at the pinned commits). The recorder ranks the density collapse first because it is upstream: even with realistic aligners and a working stack, the registered statistic would still not read placement at the registered operating point.

Feasibility.strongest_argument:
At the aligner error the literature reports for EN-ZH, the registered rule can never return the kill verdict NO_HEADROOM. The probe therefore cannot stop E3, and with correlated aligner errors it declares HEADROOM with certainty when true S is 0.90 to 0.96. Separately, the registered jobs fail on the pinned upstream code as drafted.

(1) Every threshold rests on S1's operating characteristics, and S1 models only small aligner errors. Run through S1's own generator, its noise levels low, base and high equal link AER 0.030, 0.063 and 0.126, with precision at least 0.95. Published unsupervised EN-ZH AER for these aligner families is at least 0.18:
- SimAlign without fine-tuning scores Zh-En AER 21.6 (awesome-align 2101.08231, Table 2), and awesome-align without fine-tuning scores 18.1 to 18.4.
- CTFAlign's README gives a best en-zh AER of 0.254 to 0.276, at document level with Chinese pre-segmented. The registration aligns unsegmented Chinese characters, a setting neither aligner was evaluated in.

I ran S1's own oc_part and decide() at AER of about 0.20 (drop 0.30, spur 0.20; seed 42, 2,000-pair pool, 60 replicates of 1,012 pairs, 400 bootstraps):
- **Independent errors:** inter-aligner cut Dice is 0.6625, so the verdict is INSTRUMENT_INVALID with probability 1.00 at every true S from 0.66 to 1.00.
- **Correlated errors:** this is the realistic case, because at single-sentence scope CTFAlign is SimAlign with a different encoder; its README lists `simalign` as the unconstrained base method. Cut Dice is 0.955, which passes gate I4. But a perfect system's self-ceiling S reads only 0.87 and 0.84. The verdict is INDETERMINATE with probability 1.00 at true S 1.00, and HEADROOM with probability 1.00 at true S 0.964, 0.932 and 0.903, which is the region where the registration claims HEADROOM is never declared. P(NO_HEADROOM) is 0 in every cell.

(2) As drafted, the registered compute cannot run:
- Section 13 requires fp32 with TF32 off. hnet/modules/mha.py at 3673fe12 asserts `qkv.dtype in [torch.float16, torch.bfloat16]` (lines 55 and 123), and every CausalMHA uses FlashCausalSelfAttention. The 2-stage model's inner encoder begins with a Transformer layer (T1), so the smoke job's forward pass and every stage-2 boundary fail. Under section 10 that is INCOMPLETE, with no repair allowed inside this id.
- `import hnet` fails on the pinned image. hnet imports mamba_ssm at its pin a6a1dae, whose `__init__` imports `GreedySearchDecoderOnlyOutput` and `SampleDecoderOnlyOutput` from transformers.generation. transformers 5.15.0, which uv.lock pins, no longer exports either name.

Identification.lens: Identification: whether the Stage-0 probe's verdict on EN-ZH (stage 1, rate-calibrated, PBD-normalized S) would be caused by the mechanism it claims to measure, which is translation-specific boundary placement beyond rate calibration, or by confounds, leakage or artefacts of the instrument.
Identification.strongest_argument:
At the registered primary operating point, S does not measure translation-specific placement. It is controlled by the Chinese side's density and by how often the English side marks word ends, which is a monolingual property.

1. The Chinese side is nearly saturated. The proposal says this itself: M6 and C04 give one stage-1 chunk per Chinese character, and S2 assumes EN 130 and ZH 125 bytes per sentence at N0 = 3. Registration section 7 calibrates the Chinese side to English's native stage-1 count. So the Chinese boundaries cover about 85 to 100% of its canonical gaps, against about 0.35 on the English side.
2. The floor shifts only side b, which is Chinese. Circularly shifting a near-all-ones array changes almost nothing, so floor approaches system and both S - floor and ceiling - floor approach zero.
3. The budget (about 40 per side) is far above the number of consistent cuts (about 10 to 15). The ceiling is therefore "all cuts". Every cut's side-a range is an English word gap by construction, so S reduces to roughly (1-m)(1-d) / (1-(1-m)d). Here m is the English side's miss rate on word-end boundaries and d is the Chinese density.
4. I ran the proposal's own S1 code with Chinese boundaries placed perfectly, so every cut gap is kept, at d = 0.92. S is 0.98 to 0.99 when m = 0, which is NO_HEADROOM. S is 0.78 to 0.79 when m = 0.03, which is a HEADROOM call (upper bound below 0.85, seeds 42, 43 and 44; S_truth moves the same way, so aligner noise is not the cause). A 3% English punctuation or whitespace miss moves S about 0.2, roughly seven times the 0.03 gap between the two decision lines. The same absolute miss would give S of about 0.95 under a floor that had not collapsed.
5. At full saturation S is NaN or meaningless. S1's own every-character-gap rows are NaN on the ZH-like and KO-like profiles, and the proposal never reports this.
6. No gate catches the problem:
   - I2: Bernoulli boundaries at the stage-1 rates give S of -0.001 to 0.003, so the gate passes.
   - I1 cannot fail. A permuted alignment leaves 0.05 consistent cuts per sentence against 10.2, so any system passes, including Bernoulli (permuted PBD 0.000).
   - I3, I4 and I6 do not depend on boundary density. I5 passes once the Chinese side reaches the English count.
7. The thresholds (0.88, 0.85 and the agreement gate) were tuned on S1 operating characteristics for a system with a budget near the cut count (true cuts plus 2% extras, about 0.15 to 0.2 per canonical gap) and Bernoulli rates of 0.5 or less. That regime does not include the registered operating point.

So the possible outcomes (NO_HEADROOM, HEADROOM, HEADROOM_MONOLINGUAL, INDETERMINATE) are decided by m and d, through a floor that shifts only the dense side, and not by the claimed mechanism.
Identification.what_would_change_my_mind:
Changes made before the freeze that remove the dependence on density and on the English miss rate:
- (1) Move the decision to a budget below both the consistent-cut count and the word count (stage 2 as primary, or both sides calibrated down to a common budget no higher than the number of cuts), or add a registered gate that makes the pair INSTRUMENT_INVALID when either side's canonical-gap density is above about 0.6 or when (ceiling - floor) falls below a set fraction of the ceiling.
- (2) Use a symmetric floor (shift each side separately, or the sparser side) so the floor cannot collapse onto the system.
- (3) Extend S1 to the measured stage-1 densities and show that S moves by at most 0.03 under a 3% side-a word-end miss with placement held fixed, and that the operating characteristics still hold there.
- (4) Replace I1 with an alignment-sensitivity control that preserves the number of cuts (for example, transplanting cut structures across sentences of matched length) and that Bernoulli boundaries demonstrably fail.
- (5) Score line M at the treatment's own budget (word segmentation plus matched padding), and add a translation-specific contrast that monolingual structure cannot saturate by construction, such as cuts that are not monolingual word gaps or inverted phrase-pair boundaries.
- (6) Simulate operating characteristics with correlated A and B aligner errors.

If real FLORES dev data showed the Chinese stage-1 density after calibration at 0.6 or below and floor dynamic range above 0.3, the main argument would weaken. The proposal's own M6 and S2 numbers predict the opposite.

Novelty.lens: Novelty: show that the Stage-0 design or measurement is already published, or is a trivial recombination of published parts
Novelty.strongest_argument:
The refutation rests on the trivial-recombination prong. The already-published prong failed: I found no paper that measures cross-translation correspondence of learned byte boundaries. Even so, every part of the Stage-0 design is published, and the way they are put together is the standard evaluation pipeline anyone would assemble.

The parts:
(1) The question: do two languages' segmentation units correspond on FLORES under a word aligner, as a tokenizer-quality signal? That question belongs to token alignability (2502.06468, NAACL 2025). Its Future Work section already says the score "may be applied to improve vocabulary learning for fairer multilingual tokenisers". So swapping in learned byte boundaries as the unit, as a go/no-go for boundary training, is that paper's own next step.
(2) The statistic: boundary Dice/F1 is the standard boundary-agreement measure. 2608.03599 already defines boundary divergence as 1 - F1 between models.
(3) The floor: the rate- and spacing-preserving circular-shift null is SOMBRERO's (2601.22805, Sec. 3.5). regioneR and event-coincidence analysis use the same kind of null.
(4) The normalization: S = (D - D_floor)/(D_ceiling - D_floor), with the ceiling fixed at the system's own boundary budget, has exactly the form of Cohen's kappa/kappa_M, i.e. (p_o - p_e)/(p_max - p_e). That is chance-corrected agreement scaled by the maximum achievable at fixed marginals, recommended by Cohen in 1960 (see arXiv 2203.09628; Psychometrika doi 10.1007/s11336-022-09844-y). The proposal does not cite kappa_M. Its ledger credits the budget-matched ceiling to forecast verification and the R-value, with medium confidence.
(5) The cuts: 'Consistent cuts' (no alignment link crosses the split) are the phrase-pair consistency condition from phrase-based MT. Word boundaries induced from bilingual alignment have a long SMT-era lineage: Zeng et al. 2014 (ACL P14-1128, 'word boundary information, automatically learned by bilingual character-based alignments'), Xu et al. 2004/2008, Chung and Gildea 2009 (EMNLP D09-1075), Paul et al. 2011 and Zhao et al. 2013. None of this appears in the proposal's Closest Prior Work or Novelty Ledger, which name only Conditional Unigram (2025) and 1810.01480 for translation-driven segmentation.
(6) Projection: carrying boundaries through an alignment and scoring boundary F1 is 2605.28128's method.

The only new thing is the object measured (three released monolingual H-Net checkpoints), so this is an application rather than a new design. The proposal concedes most of this itself: 'This proposal claims no method novelty'. Its ledger says 'High that the measurement idea is shared; medium that the delta is worth a paper', and its own novelty doctor expects a blind critic may judge token alignability the stronger contribution (cap 74). The engineering that makes the instrument valid is real work but not a novelty claim: canonical character gaps, the aligner-agreement gate, line M. That covers the parts that are new relative to the dossier, and none is new relative to the literature.

So the header's NO_DIRECT_PRIOR_FOUND is literally true only under the narrow unit qualifier. The 'Defensible novelty delta' is a recombination and should not score as novelty. The cap should come from the blind-discrimination rule, not a reject: no direct prior matches, and a go/no-go probe's decision value does not depend on novelty.
Novelty.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any of these would move me to refuted=false:
(a) The proposal drops the novelty claim entirely. It would say NO_NOVELTY_CLAIMED, grounded only in decision value, cite kappa_M and the SMT bilingual-segmentation lineage, and leave nothing for this lens to refute.
(b) A blind critic, given the PBD-plus-S paragraph and the token-alignability paragraph, judges the instrument a distinct contribution that the prior does not dominate. That would be evidence the recombination is not obvious to a fresh reader.
(c) A demonstration that some property of the combined instrument cannot be had from kappa/kappa_M on boundary agreement, with SOMBRERO's null and phrase-consistency cuts. The candidate is the native-versus-rate-calibrated split of budget equalization from placement under aligner noise. If S1 or a short derivation showed kappa_M-style normalization fails where the self-ceiling with the agreement gate succeeds, that piece would count as a real methodological delta.

result.closest_prior_mechanism_paragraph: Given multilingual language models that each use one shared subword tokenizer, the method asks how well the tokenizer's segmentations of two languages correspond, as a predictor of cross-lingual transfer. A statistical word aligner, with priors trained on a separate parallel corpus of up to 300,000 sentence pairs per language pair, is run for a single iteration on a multi-parallel, professionally translated test corpus that has been tokenized into subword tokens, so the aligned units are the tokenizer's own tokens. From the symmetrized alignment, two scores are derived for each language pair. The first is the proportion of subword tokens in the source language that have a one-to-one correspondence with tokens of the target language, taken per direction because it drops when the source language is over-segmented. The second is the aligner's estimate of the maximum unnormalized log-probability of the links in its last sampling iteration, averaged over both directions. Both scores are compared with distributional token-overlap measures by rank correlation against downstream cross-lingual transfer (classification and tagging tasks fine-tuned in one language and evaluated in another) and against sentence-retrieval accuracy and embedding-margin measures of cross-lingual representation alignment. The comparison spans tokenizers of different types, encoder and decoder models, and language pairs written in the same script and in different scripts. The aligner score predicts transfer better than token overlap, especially for pairs in different scripts, and is put forward as a criterion for building fairer multilingual tokenizers.

result.mechanism_paragraph: Given a professionally translated test corpus (sentences in English and in a second language) and released byte-level language models whose boundary predictor decides, byte by byte, where a new chunk starts, the method measures whether chunk boundaries fall at corresponding places in the two translations, and whether a mismatch would remain after the boundary rate is equalized. A frozen word aligner, run on the untokenized sentences, defines consistent cuts: positions between words where the alignment links split cleanly into a left block and a right block without crossing, paired with the matching position range in the translation. Every boundary is first snapped to a canonical character gap (whitespace runs collapsed, a boundary inside a multi-byte character moved to that character's start), so chunk-start and patch-end conventions that differ by one byte score identically. The statistic is a Dice coefficient: twice the number of cuts that carry a boundary on both sides, divided by the total number of boundaries on the two sides. Per language pair it is normalized as S = (D - D_floor) / (D_ceiling - D_floor). The floor circularly shifts one side's boundaries within each sentence, which preserves their count and spacing. The ceiling places the same per-sentence boundary budget on the aligner's own cuts, padding with random positions when the budget exceeds the number of cuts. S is computed for each model's native boundaries and for a rate-calibrated version whose per-language thresholds equalize mean chunks per sentence; the difference separates what equalizing the budget fixes from residual placement. A pre-registered three-way rule on a sentence-cluster bootstrap interval decides whether rate-calibrated boundaries already reach the budget-matched ceiling (stop) or clearly fall short of it (headroom). The verdict must agree under two aligners from different families, and a monolingual word-segmentation reference scored at its own budget tests whether any shortfall could be closed without translations. No model is trained; the output is a go or no-go for building translation-supervised boundary training.
